- कॉपी लिंक
जोधपुर में मौसम अब धीरे-धीरे सर्दी की तरफ बढ़ रहा है। न्यूनतम तापमान पिछले कुछ दिन से 20 डिग्री से नीचे बना हुआ है। हालांकि अधिकतम तापमान में थोड़ा उतार-चढ़ाव बना हुआ है। पिछले कुछ दिनों से अधिकतम तापमान 32 से 35 डिग्री के बीच बना हुआ है। तापमान में गिरावट से आगामी दिनों में और सर्दी के बढ़ने की संभावना है।
मंगलवार को अधिकतम तापमान 35.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया, जो सामान्य से 1.2 डिग्री अधिक रहा। वहीं न्यूनतम तापमान 18.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस रिकॉर्ड किया गया।
सोमवार को अधिकतम तापमान 34.5 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान 18.9 डिग्री रहा था। रविवार को अधिकतम तापमान 33.5 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान 19.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस रिकॉर्ड किया गया था।
पिछले कुछ दिनों से न्यूनतम तापमान में गिरावट आने से रात के समय सर्दी बढ़ रही है। सुबह हल्की ठंड के साथ धूप खिलने से मौसम सुहावना बना हुआ है। वहीं दिन में हल्की गर्मी महसूस हो रही है।
जानिए इस सप्ताह कैसा रहेगा मौसम
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार आगामी दिनों में तापमान में उतारा-चढ़ाव देखने को मिल सकता है। बुधवार को अधिकतम तापमान 34 डिग्री और गुरुवार को 35 डिग्री बना रह सकता है।
4 नवंबर से 9 नवंबर के दौरान तापमान 34-35 डिग्री के बीच बना रहने की संभावना है।
इस दौरान न्यूनतम तापमान भी 18 से 20 ऐसे में तापमान में उतार-चढ़ाव भी देखने को मिलेगा। वहीं सप्ताहभर मौसम साफ बना रहेगा।

I will say my taste reflects that of a very local Hongkonger. Truly every time I travel back to Hong Kong, the first thing I want to eat is a bowl of congee or noodles.
When I crave something from my childhood, I will go to Hung Kee (Shop B2, Block B, Kwong Sang Hong Building, 6 Heard Street, Wan Chai. Tel: 3708 8715). Asia in a dilemma over rising cooling demand
By PRIME SARMIENTO in Hong Kong | China Daily | Updated: 2026-11-04 10:16
Extreme heat caused by the looming super El Nino has created a costly dilemma for Asia-Pacific: expand access to air conditioning and cold storage without driving up electricity demand and undermining climate targets.
As deadly heat waves become more frequent, cooling needs are rising just as governments face pressure to meet their Paris Agreement pledges ahead of COP31, the United Nations climate change conference scheduled for Nov 9 to 20 in Turkiye.
"Cooling is a peak-demand problem rather than simply an annual energy problem," said Genevieve Donnellon-May, an associate research fellow at the Stockholm-based Institute for Security and Development Policy. "The priority should also be on reducing cooling demand before meeting it with more electricity."
For developing Asian economies, clean power must also be affordable enough for households, businesses and industries to use at scale, she said, making cooling both a climate and an energy-security challenge.
"Governments also need to recognize that cooling access ultimately depends on access to abundant, affordable and reliable energy," she said.
For Samuel Chng Chong Wei, a senior research fellow at the Singapore University of Technology and Design, protecting people from extreme heat should be a government priority, especially amid a changing climate.
People should be able to live, work and participate in community life safely as temperatures rise, said Chng, who also heads the Urban Psychology Lab at the university.
"A household needs to be able to afford the running costs as well as the cooling equipment. A public cooling space needs to be reachable and available when people need it," he said.
Growing cooling demand is expected to drive up energy use and emissions. Global refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment generated an estimated 4.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions annually, the UN Environment Programme said last year.
The global stock of cooling equipment could more than triple by 2050, driven by population growth, rising incomes and more frequent extreme heat, it said.
At the Global Cooling Pledge Assembly in Singapore in September, participants drafted the Global Roadmap on Heat Resilience for a Warming World, a framework to help countries build resilience to extreme heat, safeguard essential services and reduce the climate impact of cooling.
A strengthened El Nino is expected to bring more heat in the coming months. The World Meteorological Organization said tropical Pacific sea surface temperatures could reach 3.8 degrees above average from November to January.
Recent heat waves have killed people and worsened air pollution across Asia. In Southeast Asia, scorching conditions have aggravated wildfires in Indonesia, intensifying seasonal haze. In South Korea, heat waves have killed dozens of people, with Seoul's daytime temperature reaching 30.1 C on Oct 12, broadcaster SBS reported.
The University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab estimates that rising temperatures will hit the Global South particularly hard, potentially causing nearly 40,000 deaths in Southeast Asia and more than 15,000 in India.
"The human and economic impact of extreme heat events is dramatic," said Alan Miller, senior managing director of the United States-based venture fund CoolPact Capital, which supports early-stage companies in India with sustainable cooling technologies and services.
Miller said heat waves not only claim lives but also cause huge economic losses. A 2022 heat wave in India, for example, caused an estimated $14 billion in food losses due to the absence of cold chains.
"The impact of heat extremes cascades throughout the economy as hospital admissions increase, power plant efficiency declines, food losses mount, construction work is halted, roads and other infrastructure deteriorate," Miller said, noting that the effects are "not linear".
"With increasing temperature, losses will accelerate and become more widespread and longer lasting," he said.

full_text:
Rising temperatures and workplace heat stress could cost Ethiopia, Ghana and Senegal the equivalent of 2.46 million full-time jobs by 2040, threatening businesses, workers and economic productivity, the International Labour Organisation has warned.
The warning comes after new ILO-commissioned studies revealed that heat stress was already undermining employment and economic output in Ethiopia, Ghana and Senegal, with the impact expected to intensify considerably by 2040.
“The studies project that, even under a low-emissions pathway, reduced working time caused by rising heat stress could amount to the equivalent of about 2.46 million full-time jobs across the three countries by 2040. Ethiopia is expected to account for approximately 1.78 million of the projected job losses, while Ghana is expected to lose 550,000 jobs and Senegal 129,000 jobs, according to the world’s biggest labour union.
The combined annual gross domestic product losses are also projected to reach about $67bn by 2040 compared with the historical reference period. The estimated losses comprise $33.3bn in Ethiopia, $23.2bn in Ghana and $10.5bn in Senegal.
The findings indicate that the economic consequences are already being felt. In 2023, workplace heat stress associated with climate change resulted in additional losses of working time and economic output in all three countries compared with their historical baselines.
Agriculture and construction are among the most exposed sectors because of the physical demands of the work and the high proportion of outdoor employment. However, the impact also extends to manufacturing, transport, trade and services, as well as businesses and workers in the informal economy.
The scale of the impact differs across countries. In Ethiopia, well over one million additional full-time equivalent jobs were lost to workplace heat stress in 2023 compared with an average year during the historical reference period, with agriculture accounting for about three-quarters of the losses.
In Ghana, workplace heat stress accounted for the equivalent of more than 345,000 additional full-time jobs lost in 2023, with agriculture representing approximately two-thirds of the total. The figure could rise to about 550,000 by 2040 under the low-emissions pathway.
Senegal recorded nearly 72,000 additional full-time equivalent job losses in 2023, with the effects concentrated particularly in the services and agriculture sectors. The losses could reach the equivalent of about 129,000 full-time jobs by 2040.
The ILO Regional Director for Africa, Fanfan Kayirangwa, said the findings showed that heat stress had become an employment, health and economic challenge rather than solely an environmental concern.
“Governments, employers and workers need to act together, combining stronger occupational safety and health measures with social protection, climate adaptation and economic planning. Protecting people from heat means protecting livelihoods, enterprises and the resilience of our economies,” she said.
The studies identified measures that governments and businesses could adopt to reduce the effects of rising temperatures on workers and economic activity.
These include adjusting working hours to avoid the hottest periods of the day, introducing appropriate work-rest cycles, providing shade, drinking water and cooling facilities, strengthening workplace heat monitoring and occupational safety standards, and raising awareness of the symptoms and risks of heat stress.
The ILO also highlighted the importance of social protection, particularly for informal economy workers who may be unable to reduce their working hours without losing essential income.
It noted that responses would need to reflect the different working conditions and economic realities across countries and sectors, with dialogue between governments, employers and workers playing a critical role in developing practical measures.
The studies on Ethiopia, Ghana and Senegal form part of a six-country research initiative that also covers Lebanon, the Maldives and Sri Lanka.
The research was commissioned by the ILO with support from the Climate Vulnerable Forum and the Vulnerable 20 Finance Ministers, with funding from the CVF-V20 Joint Multi-Donor Fund. It combines climate projections, labour market data and economic modelling to assess the current and future effects of workplace heat stress on productivity, employment and national economies.

A confluence of events could produce coastal flooding this weekend in San Diego County at the same time that people head to local beaches to escape temperatures in the mid-to-upper 80s, the National Weather Service says.
Forecast models suggest that a high-pressure system and dry San Ana winds is expected to raise San Diego’s daytime high to 79 on Friday, 83 on Saturday and at least 85 on Sunday. The seasonal high is 73.
This will occur as the morning high tides on Saturday and Sunday climb 1.4 feet to 1.7 feet higher than normal due to the effects of El Niño and a marine heat wave that occurred earlier this year.
The tides could reach 7.5 feet to 7.7 feet, enough to cause minor coastal flooding, the weather service said. There’s also concern that a major ocean swell could produce 6-foot to 7-foot waves, which would make things even worse.
“The water will go farther up the beach if that happens,” said Samantha Zuber, a weather service forecaster.
Kevin Wallis, a forecaster at Surfline, said, “I think that’s a reasonable forecast for the larger waves in San Diego this weekend. There will be a mix of northwest and southwest swells, with the largest waves showing in South County (south of Del Mar) off the northwest swell.”
Forecast models are subject to regular and sometimes major change. Last Saturday, for example, the weather service greatly reduced projected rainfall for San Diego when the models indicated that an incoming storm had shifted direction.
But this early forecast is a matter of concern. NOAA says El Niño is still gaining strength, enhancing its ability to hit large areas. A subtropical jet stream recently formed between Hawaii and California, which will help direct some storms directly into Southern California.
Forecasters did find a bright spot, noting that recent rains will reduce the chances that the incoming Santa Ana winds will spark wildfires.

MANILA, Philippines — Nearly 600 more babies were born too early in the Philippines during the April 2024 heatwave, a new study estimates, as the country heads into another stretch of extreme heat under a strong El Niño.
Zero Carbon Analytics, an international think tank on climate change and the energy transition, estimates an additional 585 babies were born preterm during the 15-day extreme heat event, a 10% increase above average April figures.
The World Health Organization (WHO) defines "preterm births" as those occurring before 37 weeks.
Temperatures during the 15-day spell ran 2.44 degrees Celsius above normal. At its peak, the town of Iba, Zambales logged a heat index of 53 degrees Celsius, one of the highest readings of the year at the time.
Climate change, according to the organization, caused the pre-monsoon weather to be 1.2 degrees hotter, leading to a separate estimate of 263 preterm births that would not have occurred without human-caused warming.
Zero Carbon Analytics compared the Philippines' statistics for April 2024 to the country's average April based on data from 1991 to 2020, following a baseline established by the World Meteorological Organization. Results were reported at a 95% confidence level.
Calabarzon saw the highest nominal increase at 100 births, closely followed by Metro Manila and Central Luzon with around 80 births each.
Cagayan Valley, however, had the highest rise in risk: Cagayan province experienced temperatures 4.01 degrees hotter than normal, resulting in a 17% surge.
Babies born too early are more prone to breathing problems, infections, difficulty feeding and trouble keeping warm, according to the WHO.
Complications of preterm birth are the leading cause of death among children under five worldwide, and many survivors live with lifelong disabilities.
A nation at risk
The Philippines was ranked seventh in Germanwatch's Climate Risk Index, meaning that heat-specific exposure is rising faster in the country than in most parts of the world.
Between 2020 and 2024, the country experienced 36 days with maximum temperatures above a threshold linked to increased preterm birth risk. Climate change is thought to be responsible for 30 of these days, given that a 1-degree increase in temperature is associated with 4% higher odds of preterm birth.
Women and newborns living in poverty are especially vulnerable due to limited access to healthcare, mobility, and resources to support traditional livelihoods.
The Climate Change Commission warned that temperatures could reach 45 to 50 degrees in treeless urban areas during Super El Niño, which began in October 2026. The weather pattern is expected to last until March 2027 and has already brought drought conditions to various provinces in the country.

The Gauteng Department of Health has issued an urgent warning to residents heading to voting stations for the 2026 Local Government Elections, cautioning that extreme heat could expose voters to dehydration, heatstroke and other potentially life-threatening health complications.
The department urged residents to take precautions as high temperatures associated with the El Niño weather phenomenon are expected to persist across the province.
The warning comes ahead of Wednesday's election, when thousands of voters are expected to spend extended periods outdoors, travelling to polling stations and standing in queues.
The department warned that prolonged exposure to high temperatures could place additional strain on the body, particularly among people with underlying medical conditions.
"With many residents expected to spend time outdoors, travel and queue at voting stations, prolonged exposure to high temperatures can increase the risk of dehydration, heat-related illnesses and other serious health complications," the department said.
Children, elderly and chronically ill residents at greater risk
According to the department, extreme heat can affect anyone, but certain groups face a heightened risk of serious complications.
These include babies, young children, older people, pregnant women and individuals living with chronic illnesses such as hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, asthma and kidney disease.
The department explained that El Niño, a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-normal ocean temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, can contribute to hotter and drier conditions in South Africa.
"The Department cautions that excessive heat can place additional strain on the body and worsen existing medical conditions," it said.
"Some medications may also increase the risk of dehydration or affect the body's ability to regulate its temperature."
Residents taking chronic medication have been advised to continue their treatment as prescribed and ensure that medication is stored correctly, away from direct sunlight and excessive heat.
Voters urged to carry water and avoid direct sunlight
With voters expected to queue outdoors on Wednesday, health authorities have urged residents to remain hydrated throughout the day, even when they do not feel thirsty.
"Residents going out to cast their vote are encouraged to drink water regularly throughout the day, even when they do not feel thirsty," the department said.
"Carrying a bottle of water when travelling or waiting in queues is encouraged."
The department also advised residents to limit sugary drinks, alcohol and excessive caffeine, warning that these could contribute to dehydration.
People spending time outdoors should seek shade wherever possible, wear loose-fitting, lightweight and light-coloured clothing, and use sunscreen with a sun protection factor of at least 30.
Residents have also been encouraged to carry hats or umbrellas and avoid strenuous physical activities during the hottest periods of the day.
Outdoor workers and people who cannot avoid prolonged sun exposure have been urged to take regular breaks in shaded areas and drink water frequently.

Symptoms that require emergency medical attention
The department has warned residents to familiarise themselves with the symptoms of dehydration and heat-related illnesses, stressing that failure to recognise warning signs could result in serious medical complications.
Common symptoms include headaches, dry mouth, unusual tiredness, dark-coloured urine, dizziness, nausea, difficulty concentrating and excessive sweating.
Anyone experiencing these symptoms should move to a cooler environment, drink water and seek medical assistance if symptoms persist.
However, the department warned that heatstroke is a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention.
"Of particular concern is heat stroke, which is a medical emergency requiring immediate medical attention," the department said.
"Warning signs include dizziness, confusion, a severe headache, hot and dry skin, fainting and a very high body temperature."
Residents have been urged to act immediately if someone displays signs of heatstroke.
"If someone displays these symptoms, move them to a cool place and seek immediate medical assistance or contact Gauteng Emergency Medical Services (EMS) on 112 from a cellphone or 10177."
Health department urges voters to prioritise safety
The department said simple preventative measures could reduce the risk of avoidable medical emergencies as residents exercise their democratic right to vote.
"While residents exercise their democratic right to vote, the GDoH appeals to everyone to make their health and safety a priority," it said.
"Simple measures such as staying hydrated, seeking shade, wearing appropriate clothing and recognising the early warning signs of heat-related illness can help prevent avoidable health complications."
The department reiterated that residents should take particular care of vulnerable family members, especially those with chronic medical conditions, during the extreme heat.

As the government conducts preparations for El Niño, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) resumed on Tuesday, Nov. 3, the issuance of its highest heat index forecasts.
According to its forecast on Tuesday, Dagupan City in Pangasinan and Borongan in Eastern Samar, registered the highest at 44 degrees Celsius.
Five areas recorded 43 degrees Celsius, including Bacnotan in La Union, Iloilo City, Dumangas in Iloilo, Mambusao in Capiz and Butuan City in Agusan del Norte.
San Jose in Occidental Mindoro, Cuyo in Palawan, Siquijor and Guiuan in Eastern Samar recorded heat indices of 42 degrees Celsius.
A heat index of 42 to 51 degrees Celsius falls under the danger category, where prolonged exposure and continuous activity may result in heat exhaustion or heat stroke.
The weather bureau also warned that around 12 areas may experience drought by the end of November as El Niño persists. These include Albay, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Catanduanes, Capiz, Negros Oriental, Leyte, Samar, Siquijor, Southern Leyte, the City of Isabela in Basilan and Misamis Oriental.
Another 57 areas may experience dry spells, while 11 may have dry conditions by the end of the month.
Due to forecasts of dangerously high heat indices, several LGUs suspended classes on Tuesday.
Cavite City Mayor Denver Chua suspended face-to-face classes in all levels in public schools, except Cavite City National Science High School, due to an expected heat index of 42 degrees Celsius.
Mulanay, Quezon, also suspended classes in all levels in public and private schools due to the extreme heat and an expected heat index of 42 degrees Celsius.
In Himamaylan, Negros Occidental, Mayor Raymund Tongson suspended classes in all levels in public and private schools amid a forecast heat index of 41 degrees Celsius.
Masterclasses
The Department of Health (DOH), for its part, is also preparing its workforce and hospitals for the potential health effects of the prolonged hot and dry conditions.
The agency has started holding El Niño masterclasses for its employees and health care professionals to strengthen preparedness and response measures.
The classes also aim to equip personnel in regional offices and DOH hospitals with information on El Niño preparedness and the appropriate actions to take as the weather phenomenon intensifies.
In anticipation of a possible influx of patients suffering from heat-related illnesses, the agency is likewise preparing to temporarily assign personnel from other hospital departments to provide medical attention to affected patients.
Dedicated fast lanes will also be established in hospital emergency rooms for patients suffering from heat-related illnesses.
The public is advised to drink plenty of water, use sunscreen and avoid going outdoors between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. when possible.

Category B COE premiums – used to register larger, more powerful cars and EVs – also increased, but more modestly, from S$131,901 to S$132,334 – a 0.3 per cent increase.
The only other COE category to post an increase in prices was for Category E or the open category.
It increased by 0.2 per cent, from S$135,790 to S$135,998.
Open category certificates are transferable and can be used to register any vehicle type except motorcycles. Motor traders often secure them for the flexibility to register cars without waiting for the next tender exercise.
The price of a commercial vehicle certificate dipped by 0.2 per cent from S$92,200 to S$92,000.
Motorcycle COEs closed at S$10,689 – 0.8 per cent lower than the S$10,778 at the previous exercise.
The latest COE results come after the Land Transport Authority (LTA) closed its public consultation exercise on COE categorisation on Nov 2.
The exercise was to gather feedback on a proposed review of the COE system, which is expected to be completed by the first half of 2027.
Besides proposing a merger of the two car categories, other suggested changes include a fee and rebate system, in which buyers of higher-value cars will pay higher premiums compared to those who purchase mass-market options. THE STRAITS TIMES
